common_name: Bayou Sunset Louisiana Iris (Historic Warm Orange-Red Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Bayou Sunset is one of the earliest medal-winning Louisiana iris cultivars, bred in the 1940s, bearing warm sunset-toned orange-red flowers.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bayou Sunset, one of the earliest Louisiana iris cultivars to win the Society for Louisiana Irises' DeBaillon Award, bears warm, sunset-toned orange-red flowers, an unusual color among the mostly blue, purple, pink, and white Louisiana iris palette. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

common_name: King of Kings Siberian Iris (White with Green Veining and Green Shaft)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; King of Kings bears white flowers marked with fine green veining and a green shaft on the falls.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. King of Kings bears crisp white flowers etched with fine green veining and a distinctive green shaft down the center of the falls, a subtle, refined color pattern among Siberian iris cultivars, opening over narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage that remain attractive as a textural accent long after bloom ends. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go many years without needing division, and when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.
